description: We are a team of enthusiasts.
summary:
HANOS is a web app that lets anyone explore real SPHEREx data as a changing sky. You pick a region on an interactive sky dome, or enter a name or coordinates. The app fetches the real single-exposure SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA and shows them in time order, with play, pause and speed controls, plus blink and difference comparison.

It measures the object’s position and brightness in every frame. It reports an apparent motion or brightness change only as an “observed change” or “candidate”, with an Evidence Card showing the checks behind it. It never claims a discovery. A spectral explorer plots flux against wavelength across the 102 SPHEREx bands. Cosmic Sound turns real measurements into notes, with a note table and MIDI, WAV and CSV downloads.

This addresses the “Planet X and SPHEREx” challenge by making SPHEREx’s repeated all-sky observations easy to search for moving or varying objects. It matters because it makes NASA’s new data usable by people who are not specialists, with every number traceable to a real file. No mock or sample data is used.
details:
What it does and how it works. The browser sends a position to our FastAPI service. The service searches IRSA for every SPHEREx exposure covering that spot and downloads small cutouts. Astropy and NumPy then align them, convert units to µJy, and mask bad pixels using the flag names read from each file. The service measures positions and fluxes, fits motion and brightness change, and returns numbers plus rendered images. Slow archive reads run as background tasks that the page polls. Stacking is strictly per detector, because SPHEREx time and wavelength are entangled. Results are cached so the five required test targets (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), and Ethiopia's first provisional Asteroid Discovery, 2023 SY20, by our team leader in October 2023, open.


Benefits. It needs no software install and no FITS knowledge. Every image carries a data-honesty bar with release, date, detector, wavelength and flag summary. The app was built to be accessible: it has keyboard control, text equivalents for audio, and a blink rate limited to 3 flashes per second.


Intended impact. More people can look at SPHEREx data, spot candidate movers and variables, and understand the caveats. It also works as a teaching tool and as a first look that experts can verify.


Tools. Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (sky dome), Plotly and the Web Audio API on the front end. Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Reproject and SQLite on the back end. It is deployed on Vercel and Render with Docker.


What is creative. The sky dome with real constellation boundaries is the way in. Cosmic Sound plays spectra and positions as just-intonation notes, with a visible scan line and a pitch graph, and it states that sound does not travel through space. The share cards can be downloaded as PNGs with a QR code, that contains the specific coordinate links to be shared with other users, to the same view.


What the team considered. Scientific honesty came first: real data only, cautious wording, and no detection claims without evidence. Reliability was the second concern, because archive services can be slow or return errors. So the app retries errors rather than caching them, shows progress, and reuses stored real results. Accessibility, privacy (nothing about visitors is stored) and credit to the NASA and partner datasets were also considered.
